qs.q: A surgeon performs an elective low anterior resection for rectal cancer. The bowel is opened under controlled conditions with no spillage of contents. According to the CDC wound classification system, what is the appropriate category for this surgical site?
o: Class I: Clean uninfected surgical site
qs.e: Surgeries involving the gastrointestinal tract under controlled conditions without spillage are classified as clean-contaminated. Class I is reserved for non-inflamed, non-penetrating procedures, while Class III involves major spillage or acute inflammation.
qs.s: Surgical Site Infections: Types, Risk Factors, Wound Classification: MCQs

qs.q: An elective low anterior resection for rectal cancer is planned. Which combined pre-operative preparation is specifically recommended for this procedure?
o: Mechanical bowel preparation with oral antibiotics
Therapeutic enemas every two hours starting the morning before surgery
Complete restriction of all oral intake for three days pre-operatively
High-dose intravenous broad-spectrum aminoglycosides for 48 hours
qs.e: Mechanical bowel preparation with oral antibiotics is recommended for elective colorectal surgery to reduce microbial load. Enemas alone are insufficient without oral antibiotic regimens.
qs.s: Surgical Site Infections: Types, Risk Factors, Wound Classification: MCQs

qs.q: A 52-year-old man undergoes an abdominoperineal resection for a low rectal cancer. What is the most likely indication and type of stoma created in this procedure?
o: Permanent end colostomy to evacuate stool after rectal and anal removal
Permanent end ileostomy to evacuate stool after rectal and anal removal
Defunctioning transverse colostomy to evacuate stool after rectal and anal removal
Temporary loop ileostomy to evacuate stool after rectal and anal removal
qs.e: Abdominoperineal resection involves removing the rectum and anus, making a permanent end sigmoid or descending colostomy the commonest indication. A loop ileostomy is instead used to protect a colorectal anastomosis rather than for rectal excision.
qs.s: Intestinal Stomas: Colostomy and Ileostomy, Types, Care and: MCQs

qs.q: A surgical team is planning the closure of a temporary loop ileostomy in a 40-year-old woman whose primary rectal cancer resection healed successfully three months ago. What is the standard timeframe recommended for closing a loop ileostomy?
qs.e: Typically, a loop ileostomy is closed at 8 to 12 weeks once the primary disease is healed and the patient is nutritionally restored. Closing it at 1 to 2 weeks is too early for adequate anastomotic healing.
qs.s: Intestinal Stomas: Colostomy and Ileostomy, Types, Care and: MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old man undergoes an anterior resection for rectal cancer. His preoperative serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level is 120 ng/mL. What does this markedly elevated level most strongly suggest?
o: A high likelihood of synchronous polyps
An early Dukes A mucosal lesion
qs.e: Very high CEA levels above 100 ng/mL strongly suggest that distant metastases are present. CEA is useful for baseline staging and follow-up after resection, but levels do not correlate with synchronous polyps or bowel preparation quality.
qs.s: Colorectal Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Surgical Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 71-year-old man with a resected rectal cancer is being evaluated for long-term prognosis. Which of the following pathological findings is considered a poor prognostic factor?
qs.e: Poorly differentiated histology, raised pre-operative CEA, venous invasion, and positive resection margins are all recognized poor prognostic factors. Negative margins and normal CEA are favorable features.
qs.s: Colorectal Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Surgical Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 66-year-old man has a low anterior resection with a low colorectal anastomosis for a rectal cancer. What surgical intervention is typically performed to protect this vulnerable anastomosis from leakage?
qs.e: A temporary defunctioning loop ileostomy or colostomy protects a low anastomosis and is usually closed after 6 to 8 weeks to 3 months. Permanent colostomies are reserved for abdominoperineal resections.
qs.s: Colorectal Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Surgical Management: MCQs

qs.q: Following a low anterior resection for rectal cancer, a male patient complains of new-onset sexual dysfunction and urinary retention. What is the most likely underlying mechanism for these specific complications?
o: Ischemia of the perineal skin flap
qs.e: Sexual dysfunction and urinary retention after rectal surgery are caused by inadvertent nerve damage during dissection of the mesorectum and pelvic autonomic nerves. They are distinct from chemotherapeutic toxicities or staple line strictures.
qs.s: Colorectal Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Surgical Management: MCQs

ai.clinicalScope: Adult rectal adenocarcinoma presenting in low‑resource East African hospitals
ai.title: Rectal Cancer (Surgical Management)
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Rectal adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumour of the distal colon that requires careful staging and surgery. In low‑resource settings, clinicians must rely on limited imaging and adapt operative techniques to local expertise and equipment.

sections.p: Rectal cancer is a malignant epithelial tumour arising within 15 cm of the anal verge, most often adenocarcinoma.
b: Diagnosed by histology of a biopsy obtained during flexible sigmoidoscopy or rigid proctoscopy.
In low‑resource hospitals, a punch biopsy with a standard forceps is acceptable when endoscopy is unavailable.

sections.p: Staging follows the TNM (AJCC/UICC) system, with MRI as the reference for local (T) stage and CT for distant (M) stage.
b: T1‑T2: tumour confined to submucosa or muscularis propria – may be amenable to local excision.
T3‑T4: invasion through muscularis into perirectal fat or adjacent organs – requires total mesorectal excision (TME).
N0‑N2: based on number of regional nodes involved; MRI or endorectal ultrasound can assess nodal size >5 mm.
M0‑M1: distant metastases, most commonly liver; if MRI unavailable, abdominal ultrasound can screen for large lesions.

sections.p: Rectal cancer shares risk factors with colon cancer, but some are amplified in East Africa.
b: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) – rare but important.
Diet low in fibre, high in red meat and processed foods.
Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection – emerging evidence for distal colorectal tumours.
HIV infection – immunosuppression may accelerate tumour progression.
Schistosoma mansoni infection – chronic colonic inflammation can predispose.

sections.p: Patients often present late because of limited screening and overlapping benign conditions.
b: Rectal bleeding mixed with stool and mucus – usually painless.
Change in bowel habit (narrowing of stool, tenesmus).
Unexplained weight loss and anorexia.
Occult anemia leading to fatigue.
Occasional palpable mass on digital rectal exam (DRE) for low tumours.

sections.p: Select tests that answer the key clinical questions of diagnosis, staging and operability.

t.b: Is the tumour palpable and how far from the anal verge? – Determines feasibility of sphincter‑preserving surgery.
Confirms histology and provides tumour location – Guides surgical planning.

t.a: Pelvic MRI (or endorectal ultrasound if MRI unavailable)
t.b: What is the depth of invasion and circumferential resection margin? – Stages T and assesses nodal involvement.
Are there liver metastases? – Detects large lesions when CT/MRI not accessible.
Baseline tumour marker for follow‑up; may be normal in early disease.

t.a: Full blood count and iron studies
t.b: Is there iron‑deficiency anemia? – Supports chronic blood loss and guides transfusion need.

sections.p: Recognise features that demand urgent intervention.
b: Obstructive symptoms with colonic dilation – risk of perforation.
Severe anemia (Hb < 8 g/dL) causing hemodynamic instability.
Fistula formation or perineal skin breakdown in low tumours.
Rapid weight loss (>10 % in 3 months).
Signs of metastatic disease (e.g., hepatic tenderness, jaundice).

sections.p: Surgery is the cornerstone; neoadjuvant therapy is used when resources allow.
b: Upper/mid rectal tumours (≥10 cm from anal verge): anterior resection with total mesorectal excision (TME).
Low tumours (≤5 cm) involving sphincter: abdominoperineal resection (APR) with permanent colostomy.
Very low tumours (<2 cm) with good sphincter function: colo‑anal anastomosis plus temporary loop ileostomy.
T1 well‑differentiated tumours <3 cm: transanal local excision if MRI shows no nodal disease.
Neoadjuvant long‑course radiotherapy ± 5‑FU‑based chemotherapy for T3/T4 or threatened circumferential margin – may be omitted where radiotherapy is unavailable, proceeding directly to surgery.
Post‑operative care: monitor for anastomotic leak (fever, tachycardia, peritoneal signs), manage with drainage or re‑operation.

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance detects recurrence and new primaries.
b: Clinical review and CEA every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years, then every 6‑12 months up to 5 years.
Colonoscopy at 1 year post‑resection, then every 3‑5 years.
Abdominal ultrasound annually for liver metastasis surveillance when CT/MRI not feasible.
Lifestyle advice: high‑fibre diet, limit red meat, quit smoking, treat HIV aggressively.
Vaccination against HPV where available.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic rectal cancer clinically or endoscopically.
b: Rectal adenoma – benign polyp; biopsy shows dysplasia without invasive carcinoma.
Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) – chronic ulceration and pseudopolyps; histology shows inflammatory changes.
Rectal prolapse – external protrusion of rectal wall, no mass on DRE.
Anal fissure – painful bleeding, but pain on defecation and a visible fissure on inspection.

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation that are common in low‑resource settings.
b: Normal CEA does not exclude cancer – up to 30 % of early tumours are CEA‑negative.
Ultrasound may miss small liver metastases; a negative scan does not rule out micrometastatic disease.
Biopsy sampling error – superficial biopsies can miss deeper invasive carcinoma; repeat if suspicion persists.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe rectal bleeding with hemodynamic instability
Acute bowel obstruction with vomiting and abdominal distension
Signs of anastomotic leak after surgery (fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain)
New onset severe abdominal pain suggesting perforation

faq.q: Why is MRI preferred for local staging?
faq.a: MRI accurately shows depth of tumour invasion, circumferential margin and nodal size, which dictate the surgical approach.

faq.q: Can a patient with a low tumour avoid a permanent colostomy?
faq.a: Yes, if the tumour is >1 cm above the sphincter and sphincter function is intact, a colo‑anal anastomosis with a temporary ileostomy may be performed.

faq.q: What is the role of neoadjuvant therapy in low‑resource hospitals?
faq.a: When radiotherapy is available, it downstages T3/T4 tumours, increasing the chance of sphincter‑preserving surgery; otherwise, surgery proceeds directly.

exam: A 55‑year‑old man presents with painless rectal bleeding and weight loss; DRE feels a firm mass 4 cm from the anal verge. What is the next best step? — Obtain flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy to confirm diagnosis before staging.

MRI shows a T3 tumour with threatened circumferential margin but no distant metastases. How does this influence surgical planning? — Recommend neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy to improve resectability and reduce local recurrence.

During postoperative day 5 after low anterior resection, the patient develops fever, tachycardia and abdominal tenderness. What complication should you suspect and what is the immediate management? — Suspect an anastomotic leak; obtain CT with contrast if possible, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics and arrange urgent surgical review.
A patient with HIV presents with rectal cancer. Which additional pre‑operative consideration is essential? — Optimize CD4 count and antiretroviral therapy to reduce postoperative infection risk.

Why is a temporary loop ileostomy often created after low anterior resection in low‑resource settings? — It diverts feces, protecting the distal anastomosis while healing, reducing leak‑related morbidity where intensive care is limited.
What surveillance strategy is feasible where CT is unavailable? — Annual abdominal ultrasound for liver metastases, CEA monitoring, and colonoscopy at 1 year then every 3‑5 years.

A 40‑year‑old woman with a 2 cm T1 rectal tumour asks about local excision. What criteria must be met? — Tumour ≤3 cm, well‑differentiated, no nodal disease on MRI/ultrasound, and adequate distal margin.
How does schistosomiasis potentially contribute to rectal cancer in East Africa? — Chronic colonic inflammation from S. mansoni eggs can promote dysplasia and malignant transformation.
